title: How to Model Long-Term Returns Using Historical US Market Data
description: Moving beyond 'assume 10%' to understanding sequence risk, CAPE ratios, and real returns.
content:
When planning for retirement, most people plug '8%' or '10%' into a compound interest calculator and smile at the result. This is dangerous. Historical averages mask the reality of 'Sequence of Returns Risk' and valuation extremes. If you retire into a 1929 or 2000-style crash, 'average' returns won't save you. Sophisticated investors use more robust modeling techniques—like Monte Carlo simulations and Shiller CAPE valuations—to stress-test their future. This guide explains how to project returns realistically.

Key Takeaways

  • Nominal vs. Real: The S&P 500 returns ~10% nominal. But after 3% inflation, you only eat 7%. Always plan using Real Returns.
  • The CAPE Ratio: The Cyclically Adjusted Price-to-Earnings ratio predicts 10-year returns. When CAPE is high (expensive stocks), future returns are statistically lower.
  • Monte Carlo Simulations: Don't use a straight line. Use a simulation that runs 10,000 random market scenarios. Aim for a 90% success rate.
  • The 4% Rule Origin: It wasn't based on average returns; it was based on the worst historical 30-year period (1966-1995).

Why It Matters (US Context)

US market data is the most robust in the world, dating back to 1871 (Cowles Commission / Shiller Data). This allows us to model outcomes through World Wars, Inflation Spikes (1970s), and Deflationary Busts (1930s). Betting on the US market is betting that the future will rhyme with the past.

Tools for Better Modeling

Stop using simple calculators. Use these frameworks.

1. The Shiller CAPE Forecast

Professor Robert Shiller proved that starting valuation matters.

  • Low CAPE (<15): Expect 10-15% annual returns over the next decade.
  • High CAPE (>30): Expect 0-5% annual returns over the next decade.
  • Action: If CAPE is high (like in 2025), lower your return assumptions to 4-5% real to be safe.

2. Monte Carlo Simulation

Instead of "8% every year," a Monte Carlo tool (available in Portfolio Visualizer or Personal Capital) rolls the dice.

Year 1: +20%
Year 2: -15%
Year 3: +5%

It runs this 10,000 times. If you run out of money in 2,000 scenarios, you have an 80% success rate. That is risky. You want 95%.

3. Sequence of Returns Risk

A crash early in retirement is devastating. Losing 20% in Year 1 of retirement is mathematically unrecoverable compared to losing 20% in Year 20. Mitigation: Hold a 'Bond Tent' or Cash Buffer for the first 5 years.

How to Build Your Projection

  1. Conservative Baseline: Use 5% Real Return for stocks and 0% Real Return for bonds. If the market does better, great. If not, you are prepared.
  2. Range Planning: Don't aim for a specific number (e.g., $2M). Aim for a range ($1.8M - $2.5M). Life is messy.
  3. Flexibility Factor: The best model is a flexible lifestyle. If the market drops, can you cut spending by 10%? If yes, your success rate jumps dramatically.
  4. Use 'Portfolio Visualizer': This free US tool allows you to backtest your exact portfolio (e.g., 60% VTI / 40% BND) against historical crashes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the US market exceptional?

It has been for 100 years. 'American Exceptionalism' in finance is a debated topic. Diversifying internationally hedges the risk that the US century is ending.

Why not assume 10%?

Because inflation exists. A million dollars in 30 years buys what $400k buys today. Using nominal (10%) numbers gives you a false sense of wealth.

How accurate are these models?

They are guesses. 'All models are wrong, but some are useful.' They identify fragility in your plan, not the future.
